Imagine OS

The end of finished software.

Imagine OS will change how software is built. Instead of fixed apps, shipped once and learned forever, the device runs a real model locally and shapes its software around the person using it.

01 — The fixed world

Software arrives finished.

The phone in a pocket, the laptop on a desk, the row of apps waiting in a dock: all of it was decided before you opened it. Menus, icons, workflows, the shape of a day. You adapt. The software does not.

That bargain made computers useful. It also made them the same for everyone. A tool can be powerful and still have nothing to do with the way you actually think.

02 — The picture

An operating system that imagines.

Picture a machine that starts from you. You begin a task, and the interface for it is composed in the moment: the controls you need, the layout that fits the work, a small piece of software that did not exist this morning. The next day it is different, because you were.

This is not a theme, and it is not a skin over the same apps. Native software stops being a finished object. Imagine OS is that picture. It is what Boole is building toward.

03 — On the device

The model has to live here.

An interface that can imagine needs a model close enough to know you, and close enough to answer without a datacenter in the loop. Local is what makes the rest possible.

Private

The work stays on the device. Your habits are not a transcript sent somewhere else to be useful.

Instant

There is no queue and no round trip. The model is already where you are.

Offline

Once the weights are on the machine, the work does not wait on a network.

Yours

No API key and no per-token bill for the run. The runtime is something you hold.

04 — The horizon

Where it is going.

These are goals. Boole has not published a benchmark for them.

Goal

Ternary weights

BitNet-style 1.58-bit models, so a full network can live on the device rather than in a rented cluster.

Goal

20 billion parameters, 200 tokens a second

A speed target for a model of that size. A number we are aiming at. Not a number we have measured.

Goal

A shell, unfinished on purpose

The default interface is a beginning. The longer work is software that keeps reshaping itself from use, with the model still running locally.

For builders

The runtime, today.

What runs today is a command line, version 0.0.1. It runs GGUF models on your machine through llama.cpp. That local runtime is what this idea stands on.

npx @boole/cli

  • run prompts a local model. An alias such as llama3 picks a quantization that fits available memory.
  • pull downloads weights into a cache. An interrupted download resumes.
  • doctor reads the machine and suggests a size it can hold.
  • models lists the aliases.

serve and list are reserved and not implemented. If node-llama-cpp is missing, the CLI says so and stops. The source and the npm package are public. The license is MIT.
